questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/f57f1223c28fc554909be6bbd2e8eafefa21a886b1a5abb47549f17bfa12e2ab.png)

For the parabola shown above, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.
questions.worked_solution:
The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the minimum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is $(3,-2).$

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is $x=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/28032a665a1266f06292394bc9a238b196c25ef9e8d275009e3d7587a1511c6e.png)

Find the roots of the parabola shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The roots of a parabola are the $x$-intercepts of the parabola.

From the graph, we can see that the curve intercepts the $x$-axis at the point $(-1,0).$

Therefore, the root is $x=-1.$

The equation of the curve above is $y=-{x}^{2}+2x+k.$ Find the value of $k.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that if we substitute $x=0$ into the given equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}-x+k \\ y & =-(0)^{2}+2(0)+k \\ y & =k,\end{aligned}
$$

meaning that the curve intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,k).$ Based on the graph, we see that we must have $k=5$ since our parabola intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,5).$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Vertex and Axis of Symmetry of a Parabola Given Its Graph
canonical_examples.problem:
For the parabola shown below, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/e88db5363a50530228fefa2e69a9a3a0e1a62eb461103441e61af5c1f7eb6c3b.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In a downwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the maximum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is $(-2,3).$

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is $x=-2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/91e9d323945b1520aa36b70f3faf8c801e28b21437cd1008b54e76dae76d5ccb.png)

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/9e012ecda75df732e1c96ea4a52762fb085f444f41991ed9a3fe72d7d8e10025.png)

The equation of the curve above is $y=x^2+2x+k.$ Find the value of $k.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that if we substitute $x=0$ into the given equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{2}+2x+k \\ y & =(0)^{2}+2(0)+k \\ y & =k,\end{aligned}
$$

meaning that the curve intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,k).$ Based on the graph, we see that we must have $k=0$ since our parabola intercepts the $y$-axis at $\left(0,0\right).$

We say that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/78d4465d85b55cee3832a9b598a2564b6a3fa9a072de8a1fb4b40ca884079670.svg) is the **![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-intercept**. The ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/1d9b846cface9f9348e4081a0dd87dd254bf26663c12aa0d1a15aa24d2393261.svg)-intercept is the same as the constant term of the function.

- The parabola has a "turning point" at  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/ef43561f9d825c9e79fb03dffafa744d386d0c2a5a07da903675bca120d59fd1.svg) which is called the **vertex**. In an upwards parabola (like the one shown above), the vertex is the minimum point, while in a downwards parabola, the vertex is the maximum point.

- The vertical line  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/df9822243c11ec9f0fabca5cc578976d0bdea2c521b4f61964f5f3850a970504.svg) that passes through the vertex is called the **axis of symmetry**. The part of the parabola to the left of the axis of symmetry is the mirror image of the right, and vice versa.

- This particular parabola is **upward opening** because it has a distinctive ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/13ab0b72e7963f3e74404b8b75f12654ece94c2c44e1fb09fdf230b976eb681b.svg) shape. A parabola ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/7c49eede8f0eb80dadd8384ae942dc8248ef454eeb6afa1aeba7ae48e7545456.svg) is upward opening if the quadratic coefficient is positive ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/d2a0fc4d90b45e06999c89b1a40ff6f01116e9c429c195adbfced573f9e47660.svg)

- Parabolas can also be **downward opening** with a distinctive ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/57872695daf3067460adec5a506cfb1457729de4eeac879eab9f7355570bac11.svg) shape. A parabola ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/7c49eede8f0eb80dadd8384ae942dc8248ef454eeb6afa1aeba7ae48e7545456.svg) is downward opening if the quadratic coefficient is negative ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/a16d199f292dbd74941402b3d485cf107a7a985d28aeb13ab50ff6baf87f2d4b.svg)

Let's take a look at an example of a downward opening parabola.

vertex: (3,2), line of symmetry: y=3

vertex: (−2,3), line of symmetry: y=2
c
vertex: (2,3), line of symmetry: x=−2

vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=−2

vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=3
Submit
Correct

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the minimum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (3,−2).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=3.

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the parabola shown above, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.

a
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=5
b
vertex: (5,−6), line of symmetry: x=5
c
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=5
d
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=6
e
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the maximum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (5,6).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=5.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that if we substitute $x=0$ into the given equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}-3x+k \\ y & =\frac{5}{2}(0)^{2}-3(0)+k \\ y & =k,\end{aligned}
$$

meaning that the curve intercepts the $y$-axis at the point $(0,k).$ Based on the graph, we see that we must have $k=\frac{1}{2}$ since our parabola intercepts the $y$-axis at $(0,\frac{1}{2}).$

a
1
b
12
c
2

−12

32

Notice that if we substitute x=0 into the given equation, we obtain

y=52x2−3x+ky=52(0)2−3(0)+ky=k,

meaning that the curve intercepts the y-axis at the point (0,k). Based on the graph, we see that we must have k=12 since our parabola intercepts the y-axis at (0,12).

?

vertex: (3,2), line of symmetry: y=3
b
vertex: (−2,3), line of symmetry: y=2
c
vertex: (2,3), line of symmetry: x=−2

vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=−2
e
vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=3
Submit
Correct

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the minimum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (3,−2).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=3.

question.html:
Question 1
?

For the parabola shown above, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.

a
vertex: (3,2), line of symmetry: y=3
b
vertex: (−2,3), line of symmetry: y=2
c
vertex: (2,3), line of symmetry: x=−2
d
vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=−2
e
vertex: (3,−2), line of symmetry: x=3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the minimum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (3,−2).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=3.

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the parabola shown above, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.

a
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=5
b
vertex: (5,−6), line of symmetry: x=5
c
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=5
d
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=6
e
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the maximum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (5,6).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=5.

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the parabola shown above, find the vertex and the equation of the axis of symmetry.

a
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=5
b
vertex: (5,−6), line of symmetry: x=5
c
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=5
d
vertex: (5,6), line of symmetry: x=6
e
vertex: (6,5), line of symmetry: x=6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The vertex is the "turning point" of the parabola. In an upwards parabola, like the one here, the vertex is the maximum point. So, the vertex of this parabola is (5,6).

The axis of symmetry is the vertical line that passes through the vertex. Therefore, the axis of symmetry of this parabola is x=5.

solution.reasoning: The parabola reaches its maximum at (5,6), so its vertex is (5,6). Its axis of symmetry is the vertical line through the vertex, x=5. This matches option a. Question 5
?

Find the roots of the parabola shown above.

a
x=−3 and x=6
b
x=3 and x=0
c
x=3 and x=6
d
x=0 and x=6
e
x=3 and x=−6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The roots of a parabola are the x-intercepts of the parabola.

From the graph, we can see that the curve intercepts the x axis at the points (3,0) and (6,0).

Therefore, the roots are x=3 and x=6.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14217628/assets/cd847efd8b91b1c622e93b1ee97035bcee803a79a603aa7b4beee8fae77abf06.png)

The equation of the curve above is $y=-{x}^{2}+2x+k.$ Find the value of $k.$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that if we substitute $x=0$ into the given equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-{x}^{2}-x+k \\ y & =-(0)^{2}+2(0)+k \\ y & =k,\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$\,$ $x$ is not both a multiple of $5$ and a multiple of $9.$

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $5$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is a multiple of $9$
questions.worked_solution:
The given sentence is the negation of the following sentence: 

$\,$ $x$ is both a multiple of $5$ and a multiple of $9.$

The sentence above can be expressed symbolically as $P∧Q,$ and we can negate this sentence using the symbol "$¬$".

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as

$$
¬(P∧Q).
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$\,$ $x$  is even and $y$ is prime.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$  is even and $y$ is prime" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is even and }y\text{ is prime}) & ≡¬(x\text{ is even}∧y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is even})∨¬(y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd}∨y\text{ is not prime} \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd or }y\text{ is not prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $a<8$ and $a>2.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<8$ and $a>2$ " is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<8\text{ and }a>2) & ≡¬(a<8∧a>2) \\  & ≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2) \\  & ≡a\ge 8∨a\le 2 \\  & ≡a\ge 8\text{ or }a\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $a$ is odd and $b$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is odd and $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd}∧b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd})∨¬(b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡a\text{ is even}∨b\text{ is even} \\  & ≡a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}) & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}∧y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3})∨¬(y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}∨y\le \frac{1}{2} \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}\text{ or }y\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ $x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le 0\text{ and }y\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(x\le 0∧y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le 0)∨¬(y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡x>0∨y\text{ is even} \\  & ≡x>0\text{ or }y\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$\,$ $n$ is positive or $m$ is negative.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$n$ is positive or $m$ is negative" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\text{ is positive or }m\text{ is negative }) & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive}∨m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive})∧¬(m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive}∧m\text{ is not negative} \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive and }m\text{ is not negative}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
$\,$ $a$ is even or $b$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is even or $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is odd }) & ≡¬(a\text{ is even }∨b\text{ is odd }) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is even })∧¬(b\text{ is odd }) \\  & ≡a\text{ is odd }∧b\text{ is even } \\  & ≡a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
$\,$ $a<2\text{ or }b\le 1.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<2\text{ or }b\le 1$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<2\text{ or }b\le 1) & ≡¬(a<2∨b\le 1) \\  & ≡¬(a<2)∧¬(b\le 1) \\  & ≡a\ge 2∧b>1 \\  & ≡a\ge 2\text{ and }b>1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
$\,$ $x=2$ or $y\ne -2.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x=2$ or $y\ne -2$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x=2\text{ or }y\ne -2) & ≡¬(x=2∨y\ne -2) \\  & ≡¬(x=2)∧¬(y\ne -2) \\  & ≡x\ne 2∧y=-2 \\  & ≡x\ne 2\text{ and }y=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Expressing a Predicate in Symbolic Form
canonical_examples.problem:
$\qquad$ $x$ is greater than $4,$ or $x$ is irrational.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

- $P(x):$ $x$ is greater than $4$

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is rational
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sentence

$\qquad$ $x$ is irrational

can be expressed in symbolic form as $\lnot Q.$

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as 

$$
P\lor \lnot Q.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law
canonical_examples.problem:
$\qquad$ $x$ is prime and $y$ divides $12$.

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
\neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is prime and $y$ divides $12$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is prime and }y\text{ divides }12) & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime}∧y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime})∨¬(y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}∨y\text{ does not divide }12 \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }y\text{ does not divide }12.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Negating a Disjunction Using De Morgan's Law
canonical_examples.problem:
$\qquad$ $x$ is a multiple of $5$ or $y$ divides $24$.

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
\neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is a multiple of $5$ or $y$ divides $24$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is a multiple of [math]5[/math] or }y\text{ divides }24) & ≡¬(x\text{ is a multiple of }5∨y\text{ divides }24) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is a multiple of }5)∧¬(y\text{ divides }24) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not a multiple of }5∧y\text{ does not divide }24 \\  & ≡x\text{ is not a multiple of }5\text{ and }y\text{ does not divide }24.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Logical operations with predicates generalize the corresponding operations on statements. As a result, all the properties of these operations are held.

In particular, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ De Morgan's laws state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∧Q) & ≡¬P∨¬Q \\ ¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬P∧¬Q\end{aligned}
$$

These can be used to negate open sentences containing conjunctions and disjunctions. For example, let's negate the following:

$$
n \ge 0 \:\textbf{ or }\: 2 \mid m
$$

Applying De Morgan's law for disjunctions, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\ge 0\,\text{ or }\,2∣m) & ≡¬(n\ge 0∨2∣m) \\  & ≡¬(n\ge 0)∧¬(2∣m) \\  & ≡n<0∧2∤m \\  & ≡n<0\,\text{ and }\,2∤m.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
\neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is prime and $y$ divides $12$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is prime and }y\text{ divides }12) & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime}∧y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime})∨¬(y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}∨y\text{ does not divide }12 \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }y\text{ does not divide }12.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?
a<8 and a>2.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

a≥8
a<8
a≥8
a≤8
or
and
or
a≤2
a>2
a≥2
a≤2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "a<8 and a>2 " is

¬(a<8 and a>2)≡¬(a<8∧a>2)≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2)≡a≥8∨a≤2≡a≥8 or a≤2.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is odd and $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd}∧b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd})∨¬(b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡a\text{ is even}∨b\text{ is even} \\  & ≡a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?
x≤13 and y>12.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

x>13
x≤13
x>13
x<13
or
and
or
y≤12
y>12
y≤12
y<12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "x≤13 and y>12" is

¬(x≤13 and y>12)≡¬(x≤13∧y>12)≡¬(x≤13)∨¬(y>12)≡x>13∨y≤12≡x>13 or y≤12.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le 0\text{ and }y\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(x\le 0∧y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le 0)∨¬(y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡x>0∨y\text{ is even} \\  & ≡x>0\text{ or }y\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

x is not an irrational number, or x is not a complex number.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

  • Y(x): x is an irrational number

  • Z(x): x is a complex number

a
¬Y∨¬Z
b
¬(Y∨¬Z)
c
¬(¬Y∧Z)
d
¬Y∧¬Z
e
Y∨Z
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's break our sentence down into individual statements:

  • The sentence "x is not an irrational number" can be expressed symbolically as ¬Y.

  • The sentence "x is not a complex number" can be expressed symbolically as ¬Z.

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as

¬Y∨¬Z.

question.html:
Question 5
?

x is not both a multiple of 5 and a multiple of 9.

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

  • P(x): x is a multiple of 5

  • Q(x): x is a multiple of 9

a
¬(P∨¬Q)
b
P∧¬Q
c
¬(P∧Q)
d
¬P∧Q
e
¬(P∨Q)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The given sentence is the negation of the following sentence:

x is both a multiple of 5 and a multiple of 9.

The sentence above can be expressed symbolically as P∧Q, and we can negate this sentence using the symbol "¬".

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as
¬(P∧Q).

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$\,$ $x$  is even and $y$ is prime.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$  is even and $y$ is prime" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is even and }y\text{ is prime}) & ≡¬(x\text{ is even}∧y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is even})∨¬(y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd}∨y\text{ is not prime} \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd or }y\text{ is not prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$  is even and $y$ is prime" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is even and }y\text{ is prime}) & ≡¬(x\text{ is even}∧y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is even})∨¬(y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd}∨y\text{ is not prime} \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd or }y\text{ is not prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "x is even and y is prime" is

¬(x is even and y is prime)≡¬(x is even∧y is prime)≡¬(x is even)∨¬(y is prime)≡x is odd∨y is not prime≡x is odd or y is not prime.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law

solution.reasoning: De Morgan’s law gives “x is not even or y is not prime.” For integer x, “not even” means “odd,” so select “$x$ is odd,” “or,” and “$y$ is not prime.” The choices imply an integer domain for x; without that restriction, “not even” need not mean “odd.” No captured Math Academy answer or grade confirms its key.

question.problem:
$\,$ $a<8$ and $a>2.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<8$ and $a>2$ " is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<8\text{ and }a>2) & ≡¬(a<8∧a>2) \\  & ≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2) \\  & ≡a\ge 8∨a\le 2 \\  & ≡a\ge 8\text{ or }a\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

last_observation.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<8$ and $a>2$ " is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<8\text{ and }a>2) & ≡¬(a<8∧a>2) \\  & ≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2) \\  & ≡a\ge 8∨a\le 2 \\  & ≡a\ge 8\text{ or }a\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "a<8 and a>2 " is

¬(a<8 and a>2)≡¬(a<8∧a>2)≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2)≡a≥8∨a≤2≡a≥8 or a≤2.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
$\,$ $a$ is odd and $b$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is odd and $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd}∧b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd})∨¬(b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡a\text{ is even}∨b\text{ is even} \\  & ≡a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is odd and $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd}∧b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd})∨¬(b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡a\text{ is even}∨b\text{ is even} \\  & ≡a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
$\,$ $x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$

question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}) & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}∧y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3})∨¬(y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}∨y\le \frac{1}{2} \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}\text{ or }y\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?
x≤13 and y>12.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

x>13
x≤13
x>13
x<13
or
and
or
y≤12
y>12
y≤12
y<12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "x≤13 and y>12" is

¬(x≤13 and y>12)≡¬(x≤13∧y>12)≡¬(x≤13)∨¬(y>12)≡x>13∨y≤12≡x>13 or y≤12.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law
last_observation.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}) & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}∧y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3})∨¬(y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}∨y\le \frac{1}{2} \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}\text{ or }y\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?
x≤13 and y>12.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

x>13
x≤13
x>13
x<13
or
and
or
y≤12
y>12
y≤12
y<12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "x≤13 and y>12" is

¬(x≤13 and y>12)≡¬(x≤13∧y>12)≡¬(x≤13)∨¬(y>12)≡x>13∨y≤12≡x>13 or y≤12.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law

feedback.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}) & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}∧y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3})∨¬(y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}∨y\le \frac{1}{2} \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}\text{ or }y\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
$\,$ $x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le 0\text{ and }y\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(x\le 0∧y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le 0)∨¬(y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡x>0∨y\text{ is even} \\  & ≡x>0\text{ or }y\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.

So, the negation of "x≤0 and y is odd" is

¬(x≤0 and y is odd)≡¬(x≤0∧y is odd)≡¬(x≤0)∨¬(y is odd)≡x>0∨y is even≡x>0 or y is even.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$\,$ $n<0\text{ or }m>-5.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$n<0\text{ or }m>-5$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n<0\text{ or }m>-5) & ≡¬(n<0∨m>-5) \\  & ≡¬(n<0)∧¬(m>-5) \\  & ≡n\ge 0∧m\le -5 \\  & ≡n\ge 0\text{ and }m\le -5.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

n<0 or m>−5.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

n≥0
n>0
n<0
n≥0
and
and
or

m<−5

m≥−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "n<0 or m>−5" is

¬(n<0 or m>−5)≡¬(n<0∨m>−5)≡¬(n<0)∧¬(m>−5)≡n≥0∧m≤−5≡n≥0 and m≤−5.

Question 11
?
n<0 or m>−5.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

n≥0
n>0
n<0
n≥0
and
and
or
m≤−5
m<−5
m≤−5
m≥−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "n<0 or m>−5" is

¬(n<0 or m>−5)≡¬(n<0∨m>−5)≡¬(n<0)∧¬(m>−5)≡n≥0∧m≤−5≡n≥0 and m≤−5.
question.knowledge_point: Negating a Disjunction Using De Morgan's Law

solution.reasoning: De Morgan’s law changes “or” to “and” and negates each inequality. The negation of n<0 is n≥0; the negation of m>−5 is m≤−5. No captured Math Academy answer or grade confirms its key for this question.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
$\,$ $n$ is positive or $m$ is negative.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$n$ is positive or $m$ is negative" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\text{ is positive or }m\text{ is negative }) & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive}∨m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive})∧¬(m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive}∧m\text{ is not negative} \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive and }m\text{ is not negative}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ $a$ is even or $b$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
feedback.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is even or $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is odd }) & ≡¬(a\text{ is even }∨b\text{ is odd }) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is even })∧¬(b\text{ is odd }) \\  & ≡a\text{ is odd }∧b\text{ is even } \\  & ≡a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
$\,$ $a<2\text{ or }b\le 1.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<2\text{ or }b\le 1$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<2\text{ or }b\le 1) & ≡¬(a<2∨b\le 1) \\  & ≡¬(a<2)∧¬(b\le 1) \\  & ≡a\ge 2∧b>1 \\  & ≡a\ge 2\text{ and }b>1.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "a<2 or b≤1" is

¬(a<2 or b≤1)≡¬(a<2∨b≤1)≡¬(a<2)∧¬(b≤1)≡a≥2∧b>1≡a≥2 and b>1.

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<2\text{ or }b\le 1$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<2\text{ or }b\le 1) & ≡¬(a<2∨b\le 1) \\  & ≡¬(a<2)∧¬(b\le 1) \\  & ≡a\ge 2∧b>1 \\  & ≡a\ge 2\text{ and }b>1.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "a<2 or b≤1" is

¬(a<2 or b≤1)≡¬(a<2∨b≤1)≡¬(a<2)∧¬(b≤1)≡a≥2∧b>1≡a≥2 and b>1.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem:
$\,$ $x=2$ or $y\ne -2.$

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
question.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x=2$ or $y\ne -2$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x=2\text{ or }y\ne -2) & ≡¬(x=2∨y\ne -2) \\  & ≡¬(x=2)∧¬(y\ne -2) \\  & ≡x\ne 2∧y=-2 \\  & ≡x\ne 2\text{ and }y=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?
x=2 or y≠−2.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

x≠2
x>2
x<2
x≠2
and
or
and
y=−2
y<−2
y>−2
y=−2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "x=2 or y≠−2" is

¬(x=2 or y≠−2)≡¬(x=2∨y≠−2)≡¬(x=2)∧¬(y≠−2)≡x≠2∧y=−2≡x≠2 and y=−2.

EXPLANATION

De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.

So, the negation of "x=2 or y≠−2" is

¬(x=2 or y≠−2)≡¬(x=2∨y≠−2)≡¬(x=2)∧¬(y≠−2)≡x≠2∧y=−2≡x≠2 and y=−2.

solution.reasoning: De Morgan’s law changes “or” to “and” and negates both predicates. The negation of x=2 is x≠2, and the negation of y≠−2 is y=−2. No captured Math Academy answer or grade confirms its key for this question.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}, & {x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2}), & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{{x}^{2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{1-{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{(1-{x}^{2})}(1+{x}^{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(x+y)}{4}, & 0<x\le 2y,\,\,0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}, & 0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3(x+y)}{4})}{3{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+y)}{4{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<x\le 2y,\,0<y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(x+1)}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(x+1)}{4}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{8}{3}+2)-0] \\  & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}1+y-x, & 0\le x\le 2y,\,\,0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(1+y-x)}{2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 2y,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(2-x)}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(2-x)}{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(4-\frac{8}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

3.Calculating Conditional Expectations Given Joint and Marginal PDFs?

f(x,y)={1+y−x,0≤x≤2y,0<y≤1,0,otherwisefY(y)={2y,0<y≤1,0,otherwise

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of Y are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[X|Y=1].

Wed, Oct 14th @ 3:43 PM|Elapsed: 0:15Correct

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2+y-x}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5-2x}{6}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{{x}^{2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{1-{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{(1-{x}^{2})}(1+{x}^{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3(x+y)}{4})}{3{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+y)}{4{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<x\le 2y,\,0<y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(x+1)}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(x+1)}{4}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{8}{3}+2)-0] \\  & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

At Y=1, the conditional density is (x+1)/4 for 0<x≤2, so E[X|Y=1]=∫₀² x(x+1)/4 dx=7/6. This confirms my earlier answer, option d, and agrees with Math Academy's worked solution. The Incorrect grade applies to the actual submission 5/6 (option a), not to my earlier answer.

At Y=1, the conditional density is (2-x)/2 on [0,2], so E[X|Y=1]=∫₀² x(2-x)/2 dx=2/3. This confirms my earlier answer, option c, agrees with Math Academy's worked solution, and matches the submitted value graded Correct.

The normalization error remains: the stated joint and marginal densities each integrate to 2/3, not 1. Scaling both by 3/2 repairs them and leaves the conditional density at X=1 equal to 2(1+y)/3. Its mean is (2/3)(1/2+1/3)=5/9, confirming my earlier answer, option c. question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}, & {x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2}), & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{{x}^{2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{1-{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{(1-{x}^{2})}(1+{x}^{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{{x}^{2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{1-{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{(1-{x}^{2})}(1+{x}^{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

f(x,y)={32,x2≤y≤1,0<x<10,otherwisefX(x)={32(1−x2),0<x<10,otherwise

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value E[Y|X=x] for 0<x<1.

a
1+x22
b
1−x
c
1+x
d
1−x2
e
1−x22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

Note that E[Y|X=x] is a function of x.

The conditional density function of Y given X=x can be computed as

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=(32)32(1−x2)=11−x2,

where x2≤y≤1,0<x<1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy=∫x21y⋅11−x2dy=11−x2∫x21ydy=11−x2[y22]x21=11−x2[12−x42]=11−x2⋅1−x42=11−x2⋅(1−x2)(1+x2)2=1+x22.

solution.reasoning: For x² ≤ y ≤ 1, the conditional density is f(y|x)=f(x,y)/f_X(x)=1/(1-x²). Thus E[Y|X=x]=∫_{x²}^1 y/(1-x²) dy=(1-x⁴)/(2(1-x²))=(1+x²)/2, which is option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(x+y)}{4}, & 0<x\le 2y,\,\,0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}, & 0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3(x+y)}{4})}{3{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+y)}{4{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<x\le 2y,\,0<y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(x+1)}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(x+1)}{4}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{8}{3}+2)-0] \\  & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2+y-x}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5-2x}{6}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[Y|X=1].

a

23

59

EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

Note that E[Y|X=x] is a function of x.

The conditional density function of Y given X=x can be computed as

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=(2+y−x3)(5−2x6)=2(2+y−x)5−2x,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Now, substituting x=1 into the expression for fY|X(y|x), we get

fY|X(y|1)=2(2+y−1)5−2⋅1=2(1+y)3.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[Y|X=1]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|1)dy=∫01y⋅2(1+y)3dy=23∫01(y+y2)dy=23[y22+y33]01=23[(12+13)−0]=59.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let X and Y be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of X are shown above. Find the conditional expected value E[Y|X=1].

EXPLANATION

Recall that the conditional expected value of Y given X=x is defined by

E[Y|X=x]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|x)dy.

Note that E[Y|X=x] is a function of x.

The conditional density function of Y given X=x can be computed as

fY|X(y|x)=f(x,y)fX(x)=(2+y−x3)(5−2x6)=2(2+y−x)5−2x,

where 0≤x≤1,0≤y≤1. Outside this domain, we have fY|X(y|x)=0.

Now, substituting x=1 into the expression for fY|X(y|x), we get

fY|X(y|1)=2(2+y−1)5−2⋅1=2(1+y)3.

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain

E[Y|X=1]=∫−∞∞yfY|X(y|1)dy=∫01y⋅2(1+y)3dy=23∫01(y+y2)dy=23[y22+y33]01=23[(12+13)−0]=59.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=10$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{10}{1-(-0.25)} \\  & =\frac{10}{1+0.25} \\  & =\frac{10}{1.25} \\  & =\frac{1\,000}{125} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-14$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{1}{3}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-14.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-14}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =-\frac{14}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =-14\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Evaluate the series ${\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{4}{5})}^{n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

In this case, the first term is ${a}_{2},$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{2}=\frac{16}{25} \\ {a}_{3} & ={(\frac{4}{5})}^{3}=\frac{64}{125}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{3}}{{a}_{2}}=\frac{(\frac{64}{125})}{(\frac{16}{25})}=\frac{4}{5}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{4}{5})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{16}{25})}{(1-\frac{4}{5})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{16}{25})}{(\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =\frac{16}{25}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3,$ and so the sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

Computing the first few terms, we get:

$$
{a}_{3}=6{(-\frac{1}{5})}^{3-2}=6(-\frac{1}{5})=-\frac{6}{5}
$$

$$
{a}_{4}=6{(-\frac{1}{5})}^{4-2}=6(\frac{1}{25})=\frac{6}{25}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{4}}{{a}_{3}}=\frac{(\frac{6}{25})}{(-\frac{6}{5})}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }6{(-\frac{1}{5})}^{\,n-2} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(-\frac{6}{5})}{1-(-\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =-\frac{(\frac{6}{5})}{(\frac{6}{5})} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 18
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=6(0.5)^{2(1)}=6(0.5)^{2}=6(0.25)=1.5,
$$

and the second term is

$$
{a}_{2}=6(0.5)^{2(2)}=6(0.5)^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{6(0.5)^{4}}{6(0.5)^{2}}=(0.5)^{2}=0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }6(0.5)^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1.5}{1-0.25} \\  & =\frac{1.5}{0.75} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 19
questions.problem: Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3(0.5)^{4n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=3(0.5)^{4(1)}=3(0.5)^{4}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=3(0.5)^{4(2)}=3(0.5)^{8}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{3(0.5)^{8}}{3(0.5)^{4}}=(0.5)^{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3(0.5)^{4n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{3(0.5)^{4}}{1-(0.5)^{4}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 20
questions.problem: Evaluate the geometric series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2n}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1.
$$

The first term is 

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2(1)}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}
$$

 

and the second term is 

$$
{a}_{2}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2(2)}=\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is 

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{4}}{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}}={(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}=\frac{4}{25}.
$$

 

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{\frac{7}{10}{(-\frac{2}{5})}^{2}}{1-\frac{4}{25}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{7}{10}(\frac{4}{25})}{\frac{21}{25}} \\  & =\frac{7}{10}\cdot \frac{4}{25}\cdot \frac{25}{21} \\  & =\frac{2}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Given Its First Term and Common Ratio
canonical_examples.problem: Given that $a_1=-2$ and $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4$ for all integers $n \geq 1,$ find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{n}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
a_1=-2.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1-(-0.4)} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1.4} \\  & =-\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2(0.5)^{n}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is 

$$
a_1 = 2(0.5)^{1} = 1.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{2(0.5)^2}{2(0.5)^1} = 0.5.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }2(0.5)^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-0.5} \\  & =\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation With an Arbitrary Starting Index
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=2}^\infty\left(\dfrac 2 3\right)^n.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

In this case, the first term is $a_2,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_2}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}=\frac{4}{9} \\ {a}_{3} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}=\frac{8}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{8}{27}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{4}{9}\right)} = \dfrac 2 3
$$

So, the sum of the series is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(1-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3}{9} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Non-Standard Form Using Sigma Notation
canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2n}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ In this case, the first term is $a_3,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

Computing the first few terms, we get:

$$
a_3 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(3)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}
$$

 

$$
a_4 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(4)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{8} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}}{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5{(\frac{1}{2})}^{7}}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5}{128})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =(\frac{5}{128})(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3(32)} \\  & =\frac{5}{96}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to evaluate the infinite geometric series 
 

$$
\sum_{n = 1} ^ \infty  3 \left (\dfrac 1 4\right) ^ n.
$$

The sum $S_\infty$ of an infinite geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_{\infty} = \dfrac {\color{black}a_1} {1 - {\color{black}r}},
$$

where ${\color{black}r}$ is the common ratio and $\color{black}a_1$ is the first term. So, we need to determine $\color{black}a_1$ and $\color{black}r$ and then plug those values into this formula.

The first term is

$$
{\color{black}a_1} = 3 \left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1 = {\color{black}\dfrac 3 4},
$$

and the common ratio is 

$$
{\color{black}r} = \dfrac {a_2}{\color{black}a_1} = \dfrac {3 \left (\dfrac 1 4 \right)^2}{3\left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1}= {\color{black}\dfrac 1 4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Given Its First Term and Common Ratio
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given that a1=−52 and an+1an=−110 for all integers n≥1, find the value of ∑n=1∞an.

a
−2713
b
−2511
c
−2311
d
−2512
e
−94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity S∞ of a geometric series is given by the formula

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

where a1 is the first term and r is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

a1=−52.

The common ratio is

r=an+1an=−110.

So, the sum of the series is

∑n=1∞an=a11−r=−52(1−(−110))=−52(1110)=−52⋅1011=−2511

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Given Its First Term and Common Ratio
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{10}{1-(-0.25)} \\  & =\frac{10}{1+0.25} \\  & =\frac{10}{1.25} \\  & =\frac{1\,000}{125} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

In this case, the first term is $a_2,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_2}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}=\frac{4}{9} \\ {a}_{3} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}=\frac{8}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{8}{27}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{4}{9}\right)} = \dfrac 2 3
$$

So, the sum of the series is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(1-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3}{9} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Question 1
?

Given that a1=−52 and an+1an=−110 for all integers n≥1, find the value of ∑n=1∞an.

a
−2713
b
−2511
c
−2311
d
−2512
e
−94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity S∞ of a geometric series is given by the formula

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

where a1 is the first term and r is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

a1=−52.

The common ratio is

r=an+1an=−110.

So, the sum of the series is

∑n=1∞an=a11−r=−52(1−(−110))=−52(1110)=−52⋅1011=−2511

Question 1
?

Given that a1=−52 and an+1an=−110 for all integers n≥1, find the value of ∑n=1∞an.

a
−2713
b
−2511
c
−2311
d
−2512
e
−94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity S∞ of a geometric series is given by the formula

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

where a1 is the first term and r is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

a1=−52.

The common ratio is

r=an+1an=−110.

So, the sum of the series is

∑n=1∞an=a11−r=−52(1−(−110))=−52(1110)=−52⋅1011=−2511

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=10$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{10}{1-(-0.25)} \\  & =\frac{10}{1+0.25} \\  & =\frac{10}{1.25} \\  & =\frac{1\,000}{125} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=10$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=10.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.25.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{10}{1-(-0.25)} \\  & =\frac{10}{1+0.25} \\  & =\frac{10}{1.25} \\  & =\frac{1\,000}{125} \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Given that a1=−18 and an+1an=−0.9 for all integers n≥1, find the value of ∑n=1∞an.

a

b

c
−192
d
−15
e
−18019
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity S∞ of a geometric series is given by the formula

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

where a1 is the first term and r is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

a1=−18.

The common ratio is

r=an+1an=−0.9.

So, the sum of the series is

∑n=1∞an=a11−r=−181−(−0.9)=−181+0.9=−181.9=−18019.

feedback.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-18$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.9$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-18.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-0.9.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-18}{1-(-0.9)} \\  & =-\frac{18}{1+0.9} \\  & =-\frac{18}{1.9} \\  & =-\frac{180}{19}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Given that ${a}_{1}=-14$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{1}{3}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$
question.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-14.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-14}{(1-\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =-\frac{14}{(\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =-14\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}=6.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}}{8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{6}{(1-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{6}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{4}{1} \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}=6.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{2}}{8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{1}}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{6}{(1-\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =\frac{6}{(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =6\cdot \frac{4}{1} \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form ∑arn.

The sum to infinity S∞ of a geometric series is given by the formula

S∞=a11−r,|r|<1,

where a1 is the first term and r is the common ratio.

The first term is a1=52(0.4)1=1.

The common ratio is r=a2a1=52(0.4)252(0.4)1=0.4.

So, the sum of the series is ∑n=1∞52(0.4)n=a11−r=11−0.4=10.6=106=53.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\sum a{r}^{n}.$ 

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=\frac{5}{2}{(0.4)}^{1}=1.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}}=\frac{\frac{5}{2}{(0.4)}^{2}}{\frac{5}{2}{(0.4)}^{1}}=0.4.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(0.4)}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-0.4} \\  & =\frac{1}{0.6} \\  & =\frac{10}{6} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
