question.html:
Question 8
?
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of 5 datapoints with 3 features in the form of the 5×3 matrix X=[0.740.610.890.3800.61−0.92−0.03−0.87−1.2−1.61−1.281.011.020.65] where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is 0 and the standard deviation is 1). We are also given the SVD decomposition X=UΣVT where:

U=[−0.3890.167−0.3120.84−0.133−0.1740.453−0.384−0.1920.7620.321−0.749−0.3480.2320.4020.7070.3840.3590.4190.22−0.464−0.2420.7120.1660.438]Σ=[3.3290000.90000.311000000]V=[−0.5910.310.745−0.558−0.823−0.1−0.5820.475−0.66]

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components.

We should pick components based on
the amount of cumulative variance preserved
if the eigenvalue is smaller than average
the amount of cumulative variance preserved
if the singular value is greater than 1
the original number of features
.

If we wish to preserve 95% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to
2 dimensions
1 dimension
3 dimensions
2 dimensions
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible.

We should pick components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are σ1=3.329,σ2=0.9,σ3=0.311.

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is σ12∑i=13σi2=3.32923.3292+0.92+0.3112≈92.4%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is ∑i=12σi2∑i=13σi2=3.3292+0.923.3292+0.92+0.3112≈99.2%.

Thus, we obtain that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 92.4% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 99.2% of the variance.

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions, since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 95% of the variance.

In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.329,\,{\sigma }_{2}=0.9,\,{\sigma }_{3}=0.311.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

$$

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.329}^{2}+{0.9}^{2}}{{3.329}^{2}+{0.9}^{2}+{0.311}^{2}}≈99.2%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $92.4%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.2%$ of the variance.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $5$ datapoints with $4$ features in the form of the $5\times 4$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-0.36 & 1.7 & 0.25 & 1.05 \\ 0.8 & -0.33 & -1.37 & -0.53 \\ -0.51 & -0.23 & 0.05 & -0.61 \\ -1.18 & -0.96 & -0.32 & -1.01 \\ 1.25 & -0.18 & 1.4 & 1.1\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}0.477 & 0.704 & -0.239 & 0.135 & 0.448 \\ -0.291 & -0.357 & -0.764 & 0.049 & 0.449 \\ -0.217 & 0.106 & 0.24 & -0.83 & 0.442 \\ -0.55 & 0.135 & 0.445 & 0.529 & 0.45 \\ 0.582 & -0.589 & 0.323 & 0.104 & 0.447\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.041 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.967 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1.671 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0.268 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.356 & -0.757 & -0.46 & -0.298 \\ 0.454 & 0.644 & -0.416 & -0.454 \\ 0.493 & -0.1 & 0.783 & -0.366 \\ 0.652 & 0.041 & -0.052 & 0.755\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. 

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components.

We should pick components based on 
{{field-1}}.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.041,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.967,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1.671,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.268.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈57.9%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈82.1%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈99.6%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $57.9%$ of the variance,

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $82.1%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $3$ dimensions would preserve $99.6%$ of the variance.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217873/assets/5eb43d1adcfa48f0fd66cd73ea05b40a9e937399457ba8614f380502c1c632dc.png)

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to $3\text{ dimensions},$ since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $5$ datapoints with $3$ features in the form of the $5\times 3$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-0.42 & -0.33 & -0.4 \\ -0.94 & 1.07 & -0.08 \\ 1.11 & 0.12 & 1.71 \\ -0.79 & -1.51 & -0.9 \\ 1.04 & 0.66 & -0.32\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.244 & 0.013 & 0.022 & -0.603 & 0.759 \\ -0.051 & -0.763 & 0.397 & 0.405 & 0.307 \\ 0.671 & 0.439 & 0.394 & 0.235 & 0.383 \\ -0.644 & 0.452 & 0.021 & 0.57 & 0.237 \\ 0.272 & -0.144 & -0.828 & 0.305 & 0.355\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.730 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.751 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1.210 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.617 & 0.395 & -0.68 \\ 0.461 & -0.882 & -0.095 \\ 0.638 & 0.255 & 0.727\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. 

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components.

We should pick components based on 
{{field-1}}.

If we wish to preserve $85%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 
{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=2.730,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.751,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1.210.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{2.730}^{2}}{{2.730}^{2}+{1.751}^{2}+{1.210}^{2}}≈62.2%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{2.730}^{2}+{1.751}^{2}}{{2.730}^{2}+{1.751}^{2}+{1.210}^{2}}≈87.8%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $62.2%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $87.8%$ of the variance.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14217873/assets/b2f5cc8cae6fac8d24e20c045990d39d088a34df26402a7f1e5137070579de03.png)

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions},$ since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $85%$ of the variance.

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}-1.35 & 0.21 & 0.99 \\ -0.06 & -0.16 & -1.27 \\ -0.22 & -1.63 & -0.86 \\ 0.19 & 0.84 & 0.61 \\ 1.44 & 0.75 & 0.53\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}0.155 & -0.805 & -0.027 & 0.027 & 0.572 \\ -0.358 & 0.242 & 0.758 & 0.142 & 0.467 \\ -0.675 & 0.055 & -0.551 & 0.438 & 0.214 \\ 0.396 & -0.030 & 0.144 & 0.887 & -0.184 \\ 0.485 & 0.538 & -0.317 & -0.019 & 0.612\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.635 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2.034 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.940 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.279 & 0.899 & -0.337 \\ 0.716 & 0.039 & 0.697 \\ 0.640 & -0.435 & -0.633\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈58.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈92.6%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $58.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $92.6%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[−1.350.210.99−0.06−0.16−1.27−0.22−1.63−0.860.190.840.611.440.750.53].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[0.155−0.805−0.0270.0270.572−0.3580.2420.7580.1420.467−0.6750.055−0.5510.4380.2140.396−0.0300.1440.887−0.1840.4850.538−0.317−0.0190.612],Σ=[2.6350002.0340000.940000000],V=[0.2790.899−0.3370.7160.0390.6970.640−0.435−0.633].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 2.63522.6352+2.0342+0.9402≈58.0%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 2.6352+2.03422.6352+2.0342+0.9402≈92.6%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 58.0% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 92.6% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using PCA to Dimensionally Reduce an Uncentered Dataset
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}-1.35 & 0.21 & 0.99 \\ -0.06 & -0.16 & -1.27 \\ -0.22 & -1.63 & -0.86 \\ 0.19 & 0.84 & 0.61 \\ 1.44 & 0.75 & 0.53\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}0.155 & -0.805 & -0.027 & 0.027 & 0.572 \\ -0.358 & 0.242 & 0.758 & 0.142 & 0.467 \\ -0.675 & 0.055 & -0.551 & 0.438 & 0.214 \\ 0.396 & -0.030 & 0.144 & 0.887 & -0.184 \\ 0.485 & 0.538 & -0.317 & -0.019 & 0.612\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.635 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2.034 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.940 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.279 & 0.899 & -0.337 \\ 0.716 & 0.039 & 0.697 \\ 0.640 & -0.435 & -0.633\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈58.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈92.6%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $58.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $92.6%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[−1.350.210.99−0.06−0.16−1.27−0.22−1.63−0.860.190.840.611.440.750.53].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[0.155−0.805−0.0270.0270.572−0.3580.2420.7580.1420.467−0.6750.055−0.5510.4380.2140.396−0.0300.1440.887−0.1840.4850.538−0.317−0.0190.612],Σ=[2.6350002.0340000.940000000],V=[0.2790.899−0.3370.7160.0390.6970.640−0.435−0.633].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 2.63522.6352+2.0342+0.9402≈58.0%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 2.6352+2.03422.6352+2.0342+0.9402≈92.6%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 58.0% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 92.6% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

feedback.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}-1.35 & 0.21 & 0.99 \\ -0.06 & -0.16 & -1.27 \\ -0.22 & -1.63 & -0.86 \\ 0.19 & 0.84 & 0.61 \\ 1.44 & 0.75 & 0.53\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}0.155 & -0.805 & -0.027 & 0.027 & 0.572 \\ -0.358 & 0.242 & 0.758 & 0.142 & 0.467 \\ -0.675 & 0.055 & -0.551 & 0.438 & 0.214 \\ 0.396 & -0.030 & 0.144 & 0.887 & -0.184 \\ 0.485 & 0.538 & -0.317 & -0.019 & 0.612\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.635 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2.034 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.940 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.279 & 0.899 & -0.337 \\ 0.716 & 0.039 & 0.697 \\ 0.640 & -0.435 & -0.633\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈58.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}}{{2.635}^{2}+{2.034}^{2}+{0.940}^{2}}≈92.6%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $58.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $92.6%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

question.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}0.98 & 1.40 & 1.50 \\ -0.08 & 0.70 & 0.20 \\ -1.32 & -0.79 & -1.12 \\ 0.99 & -0.45 & 0.09 \\ -0.57 & -0.85 & -0.67\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.701 & 0.221 & -0.466 & 0.493 & 0.003 \\ -0.148 & 0.419 & 0.689 & 0.249 & 0.516 \\ 0.579 & 0.314 & -0.029 & 0.657 & -0.367 \\ -0.107 & -0.812 & 0.296 & 0.492 & -0.005 \\ 0.375 & -0.137 & -0.469 & 0.146 & 0.774\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.215 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.273 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.238 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.547 & -0.751 & 0.370 \\ -0.564 & 0.657 & 0.500 \\ -0.619 & 0.065 & -0.783\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈86.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈99.5%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $86.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.5%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

X=[5.6592.3611.2452.5430.071−1.476−1.128−4.766−4.2355.697−3.658−1.7041.099−4.975−3.309]

We wish to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset while still preserving as much variance as possible.

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[−0.7010.221−0.4660.4930.003−0.1480.4190.6890.2490.5160.5790.314−0.0290.657−0.367−0.107−0.8120.2960.492−0.0050.375−0.137−0.4690.1460.774],Σ=[3.2150001.2730000.238000000],V=[−0.547−0.7510.370−0.5640.6570.500−0.6190.065−0.783].

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[0.981.401.50−0.080.700.20−1.32−0.79−1.120.99−0.450.09−0.57−0.85−0.67].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[−0.7010.221−0.4660.4930.003−0.1480.4190.6890.2490.5160.5790.314−0.0290.657−0.367−0.107−0.8120.2960.492−0.0050.375−0.137−0.4690.1460.774],Σ=[3.2150001.2730000.238000000],V=[−0.547−0.7510.370−0.5640.6570.500−0.6190.065−0.783].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 3.21523.2152+1.2732+0.2382≈86.0%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 3.2152+1.27323.2152+1.2732+0.2382≈99.5%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 86.0% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 99.5% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Using PCA to Dimensionally Reduce an Uncentered Dataset
last_observation.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}0.98 & 1.40 & 1.50 \\ -0.08 & 0.70 & 0.20 \\ -1.32 & -0.79 & -1.12 \\ 0.99 & -0.45 & 0.09 \\ -0.57 & -0.85 & -0.67\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.701 & 0.221 & -0.466 & 0.493 & 0.003 \\ -0.148 & 0.419 & 0.689 & 0.249 & 0.516 \\ 0.579 & 0.314 & -0.029 & 0.657 & -0.367 \\ -0.107 & -0.812 & 0.296 & 0.492 & -0.005 \\ 0.375 & -0.137 & -0.469 & 0.146 & 0.774\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.215 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.273 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.238 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.547 & -0.751 & 0.370 \\ -0.564 & 0.657 & 0.500 \\ -0.619 & 0.065 & -0.783\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈86.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈99.5%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $86.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.5%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

EXPLANATION

We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is the direction in feature space with the most variance.

The second principal component is the direction orthogonal to the first principal component.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to standardize the data.

The standardized data matrix is

Xstd=[0.981.401.50−0.080.700.20−1.32−0.79−1.120.99−0.450.09−0.57−0.85−0.67].

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is Xstd=UΣVT,whereU=[−0.7010.221−0.4660.4930.003−0.1480.4190.6890.2490.5160.5790.314−0.0290.657−0.367−0.107−0.8120.2960.492−0.0050.375−0.137−0.4690.1460.774],Σ=[3.2150001.2730000.238000000],V=[−0.547−0.7510.370−0.5640.6570.500−0.6190.065−0.783].

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 3.21523.2152+1.2732+0.2382≈86.0%.

  • The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 3.2152+1.27323.2152+1.2732+0.2382≈99.5%.

Thus, we have that

  • reducing the dataset to 1 dimension would preserve 86.0% of the variance, while

  • reducing the dataset to 2 dimensions would preserve 99.5% of the variance.

If we wish to preserve 90% of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 2 dimensions , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least 90% of the variance.

Writing v1,v2,v3 for the columns of V and u1,u2,u3,u4,u5 for the columns of U, the reduced dataset is

Xred=Xstd⋅[v1v2], since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of V.

Note: In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset X. Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

feedback.worked_solution:
We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\text{the direction in feature space}$ with the $\text{most}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\text{orthogonal}$ to the first $\text{principal component}.$

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}0.98 & 1.40 & 1.50 \\ -0.08 & 0.70 & 0.20 \\ -1.32 & -0.79 & -1.12 \\ 0.99 & -0.45 & 0.09 \\ -0.57 & -0.85 & -0.67\end{aligned}].
$$

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.701 & 0.221 & -0.466 & 0.493 & 0.003 \\ -0.148 & 0.419 & 0.689 & 0.249 & 0.516 \\ 0.579 & 0.314 & -0.029 & 0.657 & -0.367 \\ -0.107 & -0.812 & 0.296 & 0.492 & -0.005 \\ 0.375 & -0.137 & -0.469 & 0.146 & 0.774\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.215 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.273 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.238 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.547 & -0.751 & 0.370 \\ -0.564 & 0.657 & 0.500 \\ -0.619 & 0.065 & -0.783\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈86.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈99.5%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $86.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.5%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

**Note:** In order to invert the projection and interpret any further analysis in terms of the original features, we need to know the means and standard deviations of the original dataset $X.$ Additionally, in case we have more data, we can use the means and standard deviations of the original dataset to map the new data into the original feature space.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{2x+10}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator is a difference of squares. If we factor it and then cancel out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{2x+10} & = \\ \frac{(x-5)(x+5)}{2(x+5)} & = \\ \frac{(x-5)\cancel{(x+5)}}{2\cancel{(x+5)}} & = \\ \frac{x-5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator is a difference of squares. It can be factored as

$$
4{d}^{2}-36=4({d}^{2}-9)=4(d+3)(d-3).
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{4(d+3)(d-3)}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot \cancel{2(d+3)}(d-3)}{\cancel{2(d+3)}} & = \\ 2(d-3).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: What is $\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{3-z}$ reduced to lowest terms?
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator can be factored as

$$
{z}^{2}-6z+9=(z-3)^{2}.
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{3-z} & = \\ -\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{z-3} & = \\ -\frac{(z-3)^{2}}{z-3} & = \\ -\frac{\cancel{(z-3)}(z-3)}{\cancel{z-3}} & = \\ -\frac{z-3}{1} & = \\ 3-z. & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Simplify $\frac{4{x}^{2}-8x+4}{4x-4}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator can be factored as

$$
4{x}^{2}-8x+4=4({x}^{2}-2x+1)=4(x-1)^{2}.
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{2}-8x+4}{4x-4} & = \\ \frac{4(x-1)^{2}}{4(x-1)} & = \\ \frac{4(x-1)(x-1)}{4(x-1)} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{4(x-1)}(x-1)}{\cancel{4(x-1)}} & = \\ \frac{x-1}{1} & = \\ x-1. & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
The denominator can be factored as the difference of squares: 

$$
7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}=7({a}^{2}-{b}^{2})=7(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a+b}{7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}} & =\frac{a+b}{7(a+b)(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(a+b)}}{7\cancel{(a+b)}(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{1}{7(a-b)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
Here, we take out a factor of $3$ from the numerator and from the denominator, and then use the polynomial factorization ${t}^{2}-10t+25=(t-5)^{2}.$ Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3t-15}{3{t}^{2}-30t+75} & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3({t}^{2}-10t+25)} \\  & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3(t-5)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3(t-5)(t-5)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{3}\cancel{(t-5)}}{\cancel{3}\cancel{(t-5)}(t-5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{t-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{h}^{2}-10h-15}{4{h}^{2}-4h-8} & =\frac{5({h}^{2}-2h-3)}{4({h}^{2}-h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5(h+1)(h-3)}{4(h-2)(h+1)} \\  & =\frac{5\cancel{(h+1)}(h-3)}{4(h-2)\cancel{(h+1)}} \\  & =\frac{5(h-3)}{4(h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5h-15}{4h-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: What is $\frac{{y}^{2}-9}{{y}^{2}-6y+9}$ reduced to lowest terms?
questions.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}-9}{{y}^{2}-6y+9} & =\frac{(y+3)(y-3)}{(y-3)(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{(y+3)\cancel{(y-3)}}{(y-3)\cancel{(y-3)}} \\  & =\frac{y+3}{y-3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: What is $\frac{{a}^{2}-4a+4}{{a}^{2}-4}$ reduced to lowest terms?
questions.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}^{2}-4a+4}{{a}^{2}-4} & =\frac{(a-2)^{2}}{(a-2)(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{(a-2)\cancel{(a-2)}}{\cancel{(a-2)}(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{a-2}{a+2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4{b}^{2}+16b-84}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4{b}^{2}+16b-84} & =\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4({b}^{2}+4b-21)} \\  & =\frac{(b-3)(b-4)}{4(b+7)(b-3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(b-3)}(b-4)}{4(b+7)\cancel{(b-3)}} \\  & =\frac{b-4}{4(b+7)} \\  & =\frac{b-4}{4b+28}.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring a Second-Order Polynomial in the Numerator
canonical_examples.problem: What is $\dfrac {x^2 + x - 6} {x-2}$ reduced to lowest terms?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The numerator can be factored as $x^2+x-6= (x+3)(x-2).$ Cancelling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}+x-6}{x-2} & = \\ \frac{(x+3)(x-2)}{x-2} & = \\ \frac{(x+3)\cancel{(x-2)}}{\cancel{(x-2)}} & = \\ \frac{x+3}{1} & = \\ x+3 & .\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
To reduce a rational expression to its lowest terms, we need to factor the numerator and denominator and then cancel out the common factors.

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{2x}{2+6x},$ we cancel out a factor of $2$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{2+6x} & = \\ \frac{2x}{2(1+3x)} & = \\ \frac{x}{1+3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we can have more complicated expressions which require **polynomial factorization** in order to be simplified.

No need to panic though! The main strategy is always the same: factor the numerator and denominator, and then cancel out common factors.

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x+2},$ we factor the difference of squares in the numerator and then cancel out a common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{(x+2)}(x-2)}{\cancel{x+2}} & = \\ x-2 & \end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The numerator is a difference of squares. It can be factored as

$$
4{d}^{2}-36=4({d}^{2}-9)=4(d+3)(d-3).
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{4(d+3)(d-3)}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot \cancel{2(d+3)}(d-3)}{\cancel{2(d+3)}} & = \\ 2(d-3).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Simplify 3t−153t2−30t+75.

a
3t−15t−5
b
t+5t−5
c
1t−5
d
t−153
e
3t−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we take out a factor of 3 from the numerator and from the denominator, and then use the polynomial factorization t2−10t+25=(t−5)2. Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

3t−153t2−30t+75=3(t−5)3(t2−10t+25)=3(t−5)3(t−5)2=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=1t−5.

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{h}^{2}-10h-15}{4{h}^{2}-4h-8} & =\frac{5({h}^{2}-2h-3)}{4({h}^{2}-h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5(h+1)(h-3)}{4(h-2)(h+1)} \\  & =\frac{5\cancel{(h+1)}(h-3)}{4(h-2)\cancel{(h+1)}} \\  & =\frac{5(h-3)}{4(h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5h-15}{4h-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Simplify $\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{2x+10}.$
question.worked_solution:
The numerator is a difference of squares. If we factor it and then cancel out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-25}{2x+10} & = \\ \frac{(x-5)(x+5)}{2(x+5)} & = \\ \frac{(x-5)\cancel{(x+5)}}{2\cancel{(x+5)}} & = \\ \frac{x-5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Simplify x2−252x+10.

a
x+5x−5
b
xx+5
c
x−52
d
x+52
e
x+52x+5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The numerator is a difference of squares. If we factor it and then cancel out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

x2−252x+10=(x−5)(x+5)2(x+5)=(x−5)(x+5)2(x+5)=x−52.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)}?$
question.worked_solution:
The numerator is a difference of squares. It can be factored as

$$
4{d}^{2}-36=4({d}^{2}-9)=4(d+3)(d-3).
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{4(d+3)(d-3)}{2(d+3)} & = \\ \frac{2\cdot \cancel{2(d+3)}(d-3)}{\cancel{2(d+3)}} & = \\ 2(d-3).\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: What is $\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{3-z}$ reduced to lowest terms?
question.worked_solution:
The numerator can be factored as

$$
{z}^{2}-6z+9=(z-3)^{2}.
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{3-z} & = \\ -\frac{{z}^{2}-6z+9}{z-3} & = \\ -\frac{(z-3)^{2}}{z-3} & = \\ -\frac{\cancel{(z-3)}(z-3)}{\cancel{z-3}} & = \\ -\frac{z-3}{1} & = \\ 3-z. & \end{aligned}
$$

What is z2−6z+93−z reduced to lowest terms?

a
3−z
b
6−z
c
2z−3
d
−(z+3)
e
z+3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The numerator can be factored as z2−6z+9=(z−3)2.

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

z2−6z+93−z=−z2−6z+9z−3=−(z−3)2z−3=−(z−3)(z−3)z−3=−z−31=3−z.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Simplify $\frac{4{x}^{2}-8x+4}{4x-4}.$
question.worked_solution:
The numerator can be factored as

$$
4{x}^{2}-8x+4=4({x}^{2}-2x+1)=4(x-1)^{2}.
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4{x}^{2}-8x+4}{4x-4} & = \\ \frac{4(x-1)^{2}}{4(x-1)} & = \\ \frac{4(x-1)(x-1)}{4(x-1)} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{4(x-1)}(x-1)}{\cancel{4(x-1)}} & = \\ \frac{x-1}{1} & = \\ x-1. & \end{aligned}
$$

The numerator can be factored as 4x2−8x+4=4(x2−2x+1)=4(x−1)2. Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get 4x2−8x+44x−4=4(x−1)24(x−1)=4(x−1)(x−1)4(x−1)=4(x−1)(x−1)4(x−1)=x−11=x−1.

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
The denominator can be factored as the difference of squares: 

$$
7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}=7({a}^{2}-{b}^{2})=7(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a+b}{7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}} & =\frac{a+b}{7(a+b)(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(a+b)}}{7\cancel{(a+b)}(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{1}{7(a-b)}.\end{aligned}
$$

17a−b

a−b

EXPLANATION

The denominator can be factored as the difference of squares: 7a2−7b2=7(a2−b2)=7(a+b)(a−b)

Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

a+b7a2−7b2=a+b7(a+b)(a−b)=(a+b)7(a+b)(a−b)=17(a−b).
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring a Second-Order Polynomial in the Denominator

solution.reasoning: Factor the denominator as 7(a-b)(a+b). Cancelling a+b gives 1/[7(a-b)], so option a is correct, with the original restrictions a\ne b and a\ne-b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.worked_solution:
The denominator can be factored as the difference of squares: 

$$
7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}=7({a}^{2}-{b}^{2})=7(a+b)(a-b)
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{a+b}{7{a}^{2}-7{b}^{2}} & =\frac{a+b}{7(a+b)(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(a+b)}}{7\cancel{(a+b)}(a-b)} \\  & =\frac{1}{7(a-b)}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.worked_solution:
Here, we take out a factor of $3$ from the numerator and from the denominator, and then use the polynomial factorization ${t}^{2}-10t+25=(t-5)^{2}.$ Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3t-15}{3{t}^{2}-30t+75} & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3({t}^{2}-10t+25)} \\  & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3(t-5)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{3(t-5)}{3(t-5)(t-5)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{3}\cancel{(t-5)}}{\cancel{3}\cancel{(t-5)}(t-5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{t-5}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Simplify 3t−153t2−30t+75.

a
3t−15t−5
b
t+5t−5
c
1t−5
d
t−153
e
3t−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we take out a factor of 3 from the numerator and from the denominator, and then use the polynomial factorization t2−10t+25=(t−5)2. Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

3t−153t2−30t+75=3(t−5)3(t2−10t+25)=3(t−5)3(t−5)2=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=1t−5.

solution.reasoning: Factor the numerator as 3(t-5) and the denominator as 3(t-5)^2. Cancelling gives 1/(t-5), for t\ne5, so option c is correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

Question 6
?

Simplify 3t−153t2−30t+75.

a
3t−15t−5
b
t+5t−5
c
1t−5
d
t−153
e
3t−5
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we take out a factor of 3 from the numerator and from the denominator, and then use the polynomial factorization t2−10t+25=(t−5)2. Canceling out any common factors that appear in both the numerator and the denominator, we get

3t−153t2−30t+75=3(t−5)3(t2−10t+25)=3(t−5)3(t−5)2=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=3(t−5)3(t−5)(t−5)=1t−5.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring a Second-Order Polynomial in the Denominator

question.name: Question 7
question.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{h}^{2}-10h-15}{4{h}^{2}-4h-8} & =\frac{5({h}^{2}-2h-3)}{4({h}^{2}-h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5(h+1)(h-3)}{4(h-2)(h+1)} \\  & =\frac{5\cancel{(h+1)}(h-3)}{4(h-2)\cancel{(h+1)}} \\  & =\frac{5(h-3)}{4(h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5h-15}{4h-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

5h2−10h−154h2−4h−8=

a
5h+154h−2
b
5h−154h−8
c
5h−104h+8
d
5h−14h+2
e
5h+104h+4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

5h2−10h−154h2−4h−8=5(h2−2h−3)4(h2−h−2)=5(h+1)(h−3)4(h−2)(h+1)=5(h+1)(h−3)4(h−2)(h+1)=5(h−3)4(h−2)=5h−154h−8.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5{h}^{2}-10h-15}{4{h}^{2}-4h-8} & =\frac{5({h}^{2}-2h-3)}{4({h}^{2}-h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5(h+1)(h-3)}{4(h-2)(h+1)} \\  & =\frac{5\cancel{(h+1)}(h-3)}{4(h-2)\cancel{(h+1)}} \\  & =\frac{5(h-3)}{4(h-2)} \\  & =\frac{5h-15}{4h-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

5h2−10h−154h2−4h−8=

a
5h+154h−2
b
5h−154h−8
c
5h−104h+8
d
5h−14h+2
e
5h+104h+4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

5h2−10h−154h2−4h−8=5(h2−2h−3)4(h2−h−2)=5(h+1)(h−3)4(h−2)(h+1)=5(h+1)(h−3)4(h−2)(h+1)=5(h−3)4(h−2)=5h−154h−8.
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator

solution.reasoning: The numerator factors as 5(h-3)(h+1), and the denominator as 4(h-2)(h+1). Cancelling h+1 gives 5(h-3)/[4(h-2)]=(5h-15)/(4h-8), option b, with original restrictions h\ne-1,2. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

question.problem: What is $\frac{{y}^{2}-9}{{y}^{2}-6y+9}$ reduced to lowest terms?
question.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}-9}{{y}^{2}-6y+9} & =\frac{(y+3)(y-3)}{(y-3)(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{(y+3)\cancel{(y-3)}}{(y-3)\cancel{(y-3)}} \\  & =\frac{y+3}{y-3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator
last_observation.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{y}^{2}-9}{{y}^{2}-6y+9} & =\frac{(y+3)(y-3)}{(y-3)(y-3)} \\  & =\frac{(y+3)\cancel{(y-3)}}{(y-3)\cancel{(y-3)}} \\  & =\frac{y+3}{y-3}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

What is y2−9y2−6y+9 reduced to lowest terms?

a
y+3y−3
b
y2−9y2−6y+9
c
y−3y+3
d
y+3
e
y2−3y2−2y+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

y2−9y2−6y+9=(y+3)(y−3)(y−3)(y−3)=(y+3)(y−3)(y−3)(y−3)=y+3y−3.
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator

solution.reasoning: Factor y^2-9=(y-3)(y+3) and y^2-6y+9=(y-3)^2. Cancelling one factor y-3 gives (y+3)/(y-3), for y\ne3, so option a is correct. Option b is equivalent but is not reduced to lowest terms. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem: What is $\frac{{a}^{2}-4a+4}{{a}^{2}-4}$ reduced to lowest terms?
question.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}^{2}-4a+4}{{a}^{2}-4} & =\frac{(a-2)^{2}}{(a-2)(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{(a-2)\cancel{(a-2)}}{\cancel{(a-2)}(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{a-2}{a+2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator
last_observation.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{{a}^{2}-4a+4}{{a}^{2}-4} & =\frac{(a-2)^{2}}{(a-2)(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{(a-2)\cancel{(a-2)}}{\cancel{(a-2)}(a+2)} \\  & =\frac{a-2}{a+2}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

What is a2−4a+4a2−4 reduced to lowest terms?

a
aa+2
b
a+2a−2
c
a−2a+2
d
a+2a
e
a−22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

a2−4a+4a2−4=(a−2)2(a−2)(a+2)=(a−2)(a−2)(a−2)(a+2)=a−2a+2.

solution.reasoning: Factor the numerator as (a-2)^2 and the denominator as (a-2)(a+2). Cancelling a-2 gives (a-2)/(a+2), option c, with the original restrictions a\ne2 and a\ne-2. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

What is a2−4a+4a2−4 reduced to lowest terms?

a
aa+2
b
a+2a−2
c
a−2a+2
d
a+2a
e
a−22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

a2−4a+4a2−4=(a−2)2(a−2)(a+2)=(a−2)(a−2)(a−2)(a+2)=a−2a+2.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4{b}^{2}+16b-84}?$
question.worked_solution:
We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4{b}^{2}+16b-84} & =\frac{{b}^{2}-7b+12}{4({b}^{2}+4b-21)} \\  & =\frac{(b-3)(b-4)}{4(b+7)(b-3)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(b-3)}(b-4)}{4(b+7)\cancel{(b-3)}} \\  & =\frac{b-4}{4(b+7)} \\  & =\frac{b-4}{4b+28}.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following is equivalent to b2−7b+124b2+16b−84?

a
b+34b−12
b
b+44b+6
c
b−44b+28
d
b−34b+8
e
b−24b+14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

b2−7b+124b2+16b−84=b2−7b+124(b2+4b−21)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=b−44(b+7)=b−44b+28.

question.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to b2−7b+124b2+16b−84?

a
b+34b−12
b
b+44b+6
c
b−44b+28
d
b−34b+8
e
b−24b+14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

b2−7b+124b2+16b−84=b2−7b+124(b2+4b−21)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=b−44(b+7)=b−44b+28.
question.knowledge_point: Simplifying a Rational Expression by Factoring Second-Order Polynomials in Both the Numerator and Denominator

solution.reasoning: Factor the numerator as (b-3)(b-4) and the denominator as 4(b+7)(b-3). Cancelling b-3 gives (b-4)/(4b+28), option c, with original restrictions b\ne3,-7. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

Question 10
?

Which of the following is equivalent to b2−7b+124b2+16b−84?

a
b+34b−12
b
b+44b+6
c
b−44b+28
d
b−34b+8
e
b−24b+14
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We factor the numerator and denominator, canceling out any common factors that appear in both.

b2−7b+124b2+16b−84=b2−7b+124(b2+4b−21)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=(b−3)(b−4)4(b+7)(b−3)=b−44(b+7)=b−44b+28.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $A$ has no inverse

II. $\text{rank}(A)=n$

III. All columns of $A$ are pivot columns
questions.worked_solution:
The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$  

Indeed,  a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$*$\,\times $

Since our matrix is not invertible, according to the invertible matrix theorem, it must be $\text{rank}(A)\ne n.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.*  $\,\times $

Since $\text{rank}(A)\ne n$, it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))<n,$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is a solution of the equation $Ax=0?$

I. $\text{Null}(A)=\{0\}$

II. $A$ is not invertible

III. $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$ 

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Since $v\ne 0$ and $Av=0,$ 
then $v\in \text{Null}(A)$ and, therefore, $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}.$

- Statement II is true. Since $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\},$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ then  $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis

II. $A$ is **not** invertible

III. All columns of $A$ are pivot columns
questions.worked_solution:
The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately. 

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis.* $\,\times $ 

Since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn, means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,✓$

Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we must have that $A$ is **not** invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.* $\,\times $

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{n},$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and  $det(A)=-1?$ 

I. $A$ is **not** invertible

II. $\text{rank}(A)=3$

III. $A$ has $4$ pivot columns
questions.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=3=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=-1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be invertible.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=3.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=3$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $3$ pivot columns, not $4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

- Statement III is true. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then  $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $A$ is invertible

II. $\text{rank}(A)<n$

III. $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}$
question.worked_solution:
The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is invertible.* $\,✓$ 

Indeed, according to the invertible matrix theorem, 

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A).$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)<n.$* $\,\times $ 

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{rank}(A)=n.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$*  $\,✓$ 

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/f33fde62793530cfe8970a9fea690fc71036312483ea617088a8d0a663d5133a.png)

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )$ for $\frac{\pi }{8}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{8},$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{8}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{3\pi }{8}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /8}^{3\pi /8}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi /8}^{3\pi /8}{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /8}^{3\pi /8}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\theta \,{|}_{\pi /8}^{3\pi /8}+\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /8}^{3\pi /8} \\  & =(\frac{3\pi }{8}-\frac{\pi }{8})+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =8\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =4(\frac{\pi }{2}-0)+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =2\pi +0 \\  & =2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +8(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta +24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{17}{2}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{17}{2}(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})+12(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3}))+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{2\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+12(\sqrt{3})+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+14\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\,$ for $\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4)\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/4a83949bcdf4ed8d99cac451d6db21986c24819d1601578890f86fe3df99666a.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/ed702f9d982d599fc0f175dc7d7dd022aeefc3f5463aade2a9db71313faf4866.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\pi -0)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+0+\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/98bc6f2ea4d71368226f0f784d629e98949e07005bc08158206de35a87bea520.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(9-18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi })) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{4}(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2})-9(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{8}-9+\frac{9}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi -72}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{{\theta }^{3}}{3})\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3})-2(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2{\pi }^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
