questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/e3f2350ba3651e928c65e1a78908a8f8e93cb690585a3fa16b723d1cf38a5024.png)

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{9}{2}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9}{2}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{8}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9\pi }{4}+4) \\  & =2+\frac{9\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+5{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+\frac{5(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{2}+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{13}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{13}{2}\theta -\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{13\pi }{4}+6) \\  & =3+\frac{13\pi }{8} \\  & =\frac{13\pi +24}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

                    Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = \cos(3\theta)$ and the lines $\theta = -\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/350a721c254dab3a8acb2ae54ca5be0bcde6ab036e6936939194c57ae55fe4ff.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = \cos(3\theta),$ $\theta_1=-\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{\pi}{6},$ this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\theta {|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta ){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}((\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi ))) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\pi }{3}+0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 1+2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/6bfa0990b560bcb09f2a9eb0b9542296f2a8f1c196b6740702e81c59941d66c5.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

                    Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/d7b39805131dc562e233d49a84f69d30e80ca29cb9443012032d18fdb4512054.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ as shown above.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 2\sin\theta + 2\cos\theta,$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{\pi}{2},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{3\pi}{4},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(4+8\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}) \\  & =2\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =2(\frac{3\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{2})-(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}-1 \\  & =\frac{\pi -2}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we want to find the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $r = 3\cos\theta$ and the rays $\theta_1 = 0$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as shown in blue in the picture below. Can we calculate this area using polar coordinates?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/2c7e638a338aed2155ef5bf388be1f83a3a67d2296d5be09987b099a07edacbd.png)

In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2$ is given by the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Therefore, the area of the half-circle above can be obtained as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
29∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3sin⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives A=12∫0π/2(3sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=12⋅9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

When $r(\theta )=9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve r=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π(5θ−9cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
b
12∫π/2π(3θ+2cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
c
12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
d
12∫0π/4(9θ+5cos⁡(θ))2dθ
e
∫0π(θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives

A=12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

judgments.reasoning: The area is \frac12\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}(2\cos(3\theta))^2\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}. The earlier answer agrees with both the captured Correct grade and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area is \frac12\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}(2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\pi, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The captured submission was 2\pi, my supplied wrong value, so its Incorrect grade is consistent.
The area is \frac12\int_{\pi/8}^{3\pi/8}(2\cos(4\theta))^2\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}, option b. This agrees with my earlier answer, the captured Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(4\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=2\pi, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The captured submission was 4\pi, the supplied wrong value, so its Incorrect grade is consistent.

My earlier selection e is mathematically correct and agrees with the Correct grade and worked solution: A=\frac92\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2(2\theta)\,d\theta=9\pi/8. However, option b also equals 9\pi/8, since \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2(4\theta)\,d\theta=\pi/4. Thus the single-choice question has two mathematically valid answers; the captured evidence confirms acceptance of e only.

The area is \frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}(3+4\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{17\pi}{3}+14\sqrt{3}. My earlier answer agrees with the submitted value, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area formula gives A=\frac12\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin\theta+2)^2\,d\theta, whose expansion matches option b and my earlier answer. Math Academy's worked solution agrees. The submitted option a incorrectly replaces \sin^2\theta with \cos^2\theta and differs in value by -1/4, so its Incorrect grade is justified.

The area is \frac12\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}(2+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{3\pi}{2}-4=\frac{3\pi-8}{2}, option b. My earlier answer agrees with the submitted value, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}, option a, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The captured submission was option b, 2\pi, so its Incorrect grade is justified.

The area is \frac12\int_{3\pi/2}^{2\pi}(3-3\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{27\pi}{8}-9=\frac{27\pi-72}{8}, option b. My earlier answer agrees with the submitted value, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.
The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi}(2\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{2\pi^3}{3}. My earlier answer agrees with the submitted value, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(2\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac{\pi^3}{12}, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The captured submission was \frac{\pi^3}{6}, the supplied wrong value, so its Incorrect grade is justified.
Applying A=\frac12\int r^2\,d\theta with the given radius and bounds gives option c. My earlier answer agrees with the submitted value, the Correct grade, and Math Academy's worked solution.

The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(2+\sin(2\theta))^2\,d\theta=2+\frac{9\pi}{8}, agreeing with my earlier answer and Math Academy's worked solution. The captured submission was \frac{9\pi}{8}, which omits the cross-term contribution of 2, so its Incorrect grade is justified.

The area is \frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(3\sin\theta+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=3+\frac{13\pi}{8}=\frac{13\pi+24}{8}. My earlier answer and the submitted value are equivalent to Math Academy's final expression, and the Correct grade agrees.

The area is A=\frac12\int_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}\cos^2(3\theta)\,d\theta=\frac14[\theta+\frac16\sin(6\theta)]_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}=\frac{\pi}{12}, agreeing with Math Academy's worked solution. No answer fields are present in this example; the earlier response incorrectly invented a field named A.

The interval traces the shaded inner loop once; negative radii place it to the right of the origin. Its area is A=\frac12\int_{2\pi/3}^{4\pi/3}(1+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\frac12[3\theta+4\sin\theta+\sin(2\theta)]_{2\pi/3}^{4\pi/3}=\frac12(2\pi-3\sqrt{3}), agreeing with Math Academy's worked solution. No answer fields are present.

The shaded area is A=\frac12\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4}(2\sin\theta+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta=\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4}(2+2\sin(2\theta))\,d\theta=[2\theta-\cos(2\theta)]_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4}=\frac{\pi}{2}-1=\frac{\pi-2}{2}. Math Academy's worked solution is correct. No answer fields are present.

question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
29∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3sin⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives A=12∫0π/2(3sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=12⋅9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose
last_observation.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
29∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3sin⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives A=12∫0π/2(3sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=12⋅9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by a Petal of a Polar Rose

solution.reasoning: The polar area formula gives A=\frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(3\sin(2\theta))^2\,d\theta=\frac92\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2(2\theta)\,d\theta, so select e. Its value is 9\pi/8. Option b also evaluates to 9\pi/8 because both sine-squared integrals equal \pi/4, making it numerically valid too. No current Math Academy answer key or grade is captured.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 9{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following gives the area bounded by graph of the polar curve r=3sin⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
29∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
b
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
c
3∫0π/2sin2⁡(4θ)dθ
d
9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
e
92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3sin⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives A=12∫0π/2(3sin⁡(2θ))2dθ=12⋅9∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ=92∫0π/2sin2⁡(2θ)dθ.

question.name: Question 6
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{3}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(3+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +16{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}(9+24\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +8(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta +24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(17\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+24\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{17}{2}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3}+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /3}^{\pi /3} \\  & =\frac{17}{2}(\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{3})+12(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{3}))+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{2\pi }{3})) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+12(\sqrt{3})+2(\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{17\pi }{3}+14\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ+2 for π4≤θ≤π?

a
12∫π/4π(cos2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
b
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
c
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4)dθ
d
12∫0π(cos2⁡θ+2cos⁡θ+4)dθ
e
12∫π/23π/4(4sin⁡θ+4)2dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=sin⁡θ+2, θ1=π4 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫π/4π(sin⁡θ+2)2dθ=12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ.

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
last_observation.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4)\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ+2 for π4≤θ≤π?

a
12∫π/4π(cos2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
b
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
c
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4)dθ
d
12∫0π(cos2⁡θ+2cos⁡θ+4)dθ
e
12∫π/23π/4(4sin⁡θ+4)2dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=sin⁡θ+2, θ1=π4 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫π/4π(sin⁡θ+2)2dθ=12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon

solution.reasoning: The polar area formula gives A=\frac12\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi}(\sin\theta+2)^2\,d\theta. Expanding the square gives \sin^2\theta+4\sin\theta+4, matching option b. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\,$ for $\,\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \pi ?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2$, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2)^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi }({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +4)\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by the graph of the polar curve r=sin⁡θ+2 for π4≤θ≤π?

a
12∫π/4π(cos2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
b
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ
c
12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4)dθ
d
12∫0π(cos2⁡θ+2cos⁡θ+4)dθ
e
12∫π/23π/4(4sin⁡θ+4)2dθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=sin⁡θ+2, θ1=π4 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫π/4π(sin⁡θ+2)2dθ=12∫π/4π(sin2⁡θ+4sin⁡θ+4)dθ.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/4a83949bcdf4ed8d99cac451d6db21986c24819d1601578890f86fe3df99666a.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=2+2cos⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, as shown above.

a
3π2
b
3π−82
c
3π+82
d
3π+42
e
3π+84
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=2+2cos⁡θ, θ1=π2 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫π/2π(2+2cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫π/2π(4+8cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ)dθ=42∫π/2π(1+2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12∫π/2π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12(θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π))=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)4|π/2π)=3θ|π/2π+4sin⁡θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π=3(π−π2)+4(sin⁡(π)−sin⁡(π2))+12(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(π))=3π2−4+12(0)=3π−82.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
last_observation.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{4}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi })) \\  & =2(\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }) \\  & =3\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =3(\pi -\frac{\pi }{2})+4(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))+\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{2}-4+\frac{1}{2}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi -8}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=2+2cos⁡θ for π2≤θ≤π, as shown above.

a
3π2
b
3π−82
c
3π+82
d
3π+42
e
3π+84
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=2+2cos⁡θ, θ1=π2 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫π/2π(2+2cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫π/2π(4+8cos⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ)dθ=42∫π/2π(1+2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12∫π/2π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12(θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π))=2(θ|π/2π+2sin⁡θ|π/2π+12θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)4|π/2π)=3θ|π/2π+4sin⁡θ|π/2π+sin⁡(2θ)2|π/2π=3(π−π2)+4(sin⁡(π)−sin⁡(π2))+12(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(π))=3π2−4+12(0)=3π−82.

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/ed702f9d982d599fc0f175dc7d7dd022aeefc3f5463aade2a9db71313faf4866.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi })) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4}(\pi -0)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡0)+\frac{1}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}+0+\frac{1}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{3\pi }{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=1+cos⁡θ, θ1=0 and θ2=π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫0π(1+cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫0π(1+2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=12(θ|0π+2sin⁡θ|0π+12∫0π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=12(θ|0π+2sin⁡θ|0π+12(θ|0π+12sin⁡(2θ)|0π))=34θ|0π+sin⁡θ|0π+18sin⁡(2θ)|0π=34(π−0)+(sin⁡π−sin⁡0)+18(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡0)=3π4+0+18(0)=3π4.

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(9-18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi })) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{4}(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2})-9(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{8}-9+\frac{9}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi -72}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=3−3cos⁡θ for 3π2≤θ≤2π, as shown above.

a
 27π−98
b
 27π−728
c
 9π+728
d
 9π+248
e
 π−94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3−3cos⁡θ, θ1=3π2 and θ2=2π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫3π/22π(3−3cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫3π/22π(9−18cos⁡θ+9cos2⁡θ)dθ=92∫3π/22π(1−2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12∫3π/22π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12(θ|3π/22π+sin⁡(2θ)2|3π/22π))=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12θ|3π/22π+sin⁡(2θ)4|3π/22π)=274θ|3π/22π−9sin⁡θ|3π/22π+9sin⁡(2θ)8|3π/22π=274(2π−3π2)−9(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(3π2))+98(sin⁡(4π)−sin⁡(3π))=27π8−9+98(0)=27π−728.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(9-18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi })) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{4}(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2})-9(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{8}-9+\frac{9}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi -72}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Find the area bounded by the polar curve r=3−3cos⁡θ for 3π2≤θ≤2π, as shown above.

a
 27π−98
b
 27π−728
c
 9π+728
d
 9π+248
e
 π−94
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=3−3cos⁡θ, θ1=3π2 and θ2=2π, this gives

A=12∫θ1θ2r2dθ=12∫3π/22π(3−3cos⁡θ)2dθ=12∫3π/22π(9−18cos⁡θ+9cos2⁡θ)dθ=92∫3π/22π(1−2cos⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12∫3π/22π(1+cos⁡(2θ))dθ)=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12(θ|3π/22π+sin⁡(2θ)2|3π/22π))=92(θ|3π/22π−2sin⁡θ|3π/22π+12θ|3π/22π+sin⁡(2θ)4|3π/22π)=274θ|3π/22π−9sin⁡θ|3π/22π+9sin⁡(2θ)8|3π/22π=274(2π−3π2)−9(sin⁡(2π)−sin⁡(3π2))+98(sin⁡(4π)−sin⁡(3π))=27π8−9+98(0)=27π−728.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/98bc6f2ea4d71368226f0f784d629e98949e07005bc08158206de35a87bea520.png)

Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $\frac{3\pi }{2}\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ as shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=\frac{3\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=2\pi $, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(9-18\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +9{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1-2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{2}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi })) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{1}{2}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{4}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }) \\  & =\frac{27}{4}\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }-9\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }+\frac{9\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )}{8}\,{|}_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{27}{4}(2\pi -\frac{3\pi }{2})-9(\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )) \\  & =\frac{27\pi }{8}-9+\frac{9}{8}(0) \\  & =\frac{27\pi -72}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

$A=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\pi $, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(2\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\theta }^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2(\frac{{\theta }^{3}}{3})\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =2(\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3})-2(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}) \\  & =\frac{2{\pi }^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve r=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π(5θ−9cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
b
12∫π/2π(3θ+2cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
c
12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
d
12∫0π/4(9θ+5cos⁡(θ))2dθ
e
∫0π(θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives

A=12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ.

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves
last_observation.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 13
?

Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve r=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ) for 0≤θ≤π2?

a
∫0π(5θ−9cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
b
12∫π/2π(3θ+2cos⁡(5θ))2dθ
c
12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
d
12∫0π/4(9θ+5cos⁡(θ))2dθ
e
∫0π(θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The area bounded by a polar curve is given by A=12∫θ1θ2r2(θ)dθ.

When r(θ)=9θ+5cos⁡(2θ), θ1=0 and θ2=π2, this gives

A=12∫0π/2(9θ+5cos⁡(2θ))2dθ.
question.knowledge_point: Finding Areas Bounded by Other Polar Curves

solution.reasoning: The polar area formula is A=\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r(\theta)^2\,d\theta. Substituting the given radius and bounds gives \frac12\int_0^{\pi/2}(9\theta+5\cos(2\theta))^2\,d\theta, matching option c. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Which of the following gives the total area enclosed by graph of the polar curve $r=9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(9\theta +5\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14217747/assets/e3f2350ba3651e928c65e1a78908a8f8e93cb690585a3fa16b723d1cf38a5024.png)

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

When $r(\theta )=2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(2+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )+\frac{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta )}{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{9}{2}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9}{2}\theta -2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )}{8}){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{9\pi }{4}+4) \\  & =2+\frac{9\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$
